#### ! Scenario

*Or what to do when the upstream POM is wrong*
This scenario demonstrates how to correct a library's declared dependencies from your own build when the published metadata is wrong.

::: {.callout-note title="Tool Versions"}
This scenario was tested with **sbt 1.12**, which uses the **Coursier** resolver (the default since sbt 1.3). On sbt 1.x the older Ivy engine can still be selected with `useCoursier := false`; under Ivy, resolution edge cases differ and Ivy-only settings such as `conflictManager` apply (Coursier ignores them). `dependencyTree` is built in since **sbt 1.4**; earlier versions need the sbt-dependency-graph plugin. sbt 2.0 (June 2026) keeps these resolution rules, removes the Ivy opt-out, adds native BOM import, and turns Test-configuration eviction warnings into errors; the demos here target sbt 1.x.
:::

#### ! Example

```{mermaid}
%%| fig-width: 4.4
graph LR
    Root[Project Root] --> LibA[lib-a:1.0.0]
    LibA -.->|excluded| LibB1[lib-b:1.0.0]
    Root --> LibB2[lib-b:2.0.0]
    LibB2 --> LibC2[lib-c:2.0.0]
```

```{.scala include="build.sbt" snippet="s12-deps"}
```

#### ! Expect
"The library author made a mistake in their POM. I should be able to patch it locally."

#### ! Actual
You can, but not by editing the metadata. sbt has no metadata-rules API; the correction is expressed as an exclusion plus a direct declaration. The classpath ends up with `lib-a:1.0.0`, `lib-b:2.0.0` and `lib-c:2.0.0`, and `lib-b:1.0.0` never appears.

#### ! Why
Gradle lets you rewrite a module's metadata as it is read (component metadata rules, GS12). Maven and sbt do not; they take the POM as published. In sbt the workaround composes two existing mechanisms: `.exclude` removes the declaration you disagree with (SB5), and a direct `libraryDependencies` entry supplies the one you want. If only the *version* is wrong, `dependencyOverrides` (SB6) is simpler and does not need the exclusion.

#### ! Fix
*   **Wrong dependency:** exclude it and declare the right one, as shown.
*   **Wrong version only:** `dependencyOverrides += "com.demo" % "lib-b" % "2.0.0"`.
*   **Upstream:** file the issue against the library. Every local workaround is debt until the published POM is fixed.

#### ! Risk
* LOW A commented exclude-and-add pair with a link to the upstream issue.
* MEDIUM The workaround outliving the upstream fix, so the build keeps overriding a POM that is now correct.
* HIGH Patching a dependency's declared version to something the library was never built against; `NoSuchMethodError` at runtime.

#### ! Control
Keep metadata workarounds together, each with the upstream issue number. When the library ships a corrected POM, remove the workaround in the same pull request that upgrades it.

#### ! Check
**Fast check:** `sbt dependencyTree`

**What to look for:** `lib-a:1.0.0` with no `lib-b` beneath it, and `lib-b:2.0.0` → `lib-c:2.0.0` as a direct branch from the root.

**Conclusion:** The exclude-and-add pair rewrites the effective graph without touching the published POM.

#### ! Scales
In large projects metadata workarounds accumulate and become hard to track. Document each one with the reason and the upstream issue; when the library releases a fix, clean up the workaround.

#### ! Takeaway
sbt cannot edit metadata on the way in. Exclude the wrong declaration and add the right one, and record why.

#### ! Wild

The classic wrong POM is `log4j:log4j:1.2.15`, which declared dependencies on `javax.jms:jms`, `com.sun.jdmk:jmxtools` and `com.sun.jmx:jmxri`, artifacts that were never published to Maven Central. Every build that pulled in log4j 1.2.15 transitively failed to resolve until it excluded those three, which is how a generation of Java and Scala developers learned the exclude-and-add pattern. The fix shipped in 1.2.16 with the dependencies marked optional; the exclusions lived on in build files for years afterwards.
